_about: Strength goal profiles. A profile says how many sessions a week, which movement patterns each session trains (in priority order), and the set/rep/rest prescription per exercise kind. Slots are kept in priority order: preferences.strength.version short = 3 slots, mid = 4, full = all. Each number carries an evidence label in the 'basis' lines: research = a paper in this library supports the DIRECTION; practice = a convention or a choice of this planner with no paper read for the exact number. The planner never claims more than the label.

endurance.label: Endurance (running, cycling): better economy and injury resistance without costing the key aerobic sessions
basis: research: strength training improves distance-running and cycling economy and performance; maximal-force work gave larger gains than other intensities (Berryman 2018, Blagrove 2018, Rønnestad & Mujika 2014)
research: 2-3 sessions a week for runners (Blagrove 2018); strength at least 3 h after cardio (Schumann 2022)

research: more weekly sets gave greater strength gains, but gains were similar from 1, 3 or 5 sets per exercise in trained men (Ralston 2017, Schoenfeld 2019); the number of exercises per session did not change sprint transfer (Seitz 2014)
practice: which movement patterns and how many slots; weekly set targets

sessions.name: lower body
sessions.why: Strength work improves running and cycling economy: you use less energy at the same speed, and it makes the legs more resistant to overuse. The lower-body day goes after an easy day and before easy days, not before a key session.
sessions.check: Last 2 reps hard, 2-3 left in reserve. Pain is a stop sign. Note the weight and reps (Garmin stores them) so the next plan can build on them.

sessions.name: upper body and trunk
sessions.why: Upper body and core work keeps your posture strong on the bike and your running form steady late in a session. Legs stay light because a long run or ride follows.
sessions.check: Controlled reps, no shoulder pain. You should feel fresh the next morning.

sprint.label: Sprint and power (acceleration, top speed): strength is a main driver, so more sessions and heavier loading
basis: research: gains in lower-body (back squat) strength transferred to sprint performance, r = -0.77 between squat-strength effect size and sprint effect size; frequency per week and the rest between sets moderated the effect; number of exercises per session, sets per exercise and % of 1RM did not (Seitz 2014, abstract)

research: high-level sprinters usually do strength and power work 2-3 times a week in the preparation period, with sprint-specific lifts (split squats, single-leg deadlifts, lunges, step-ups), and mostly place strength the day after sprint-specific training; ballistic loads up to about 60% 1RM give high power, heavier loads are needed for the force part (Haugen 2019 review: expert synthesis, not a trial)
research: horizontal force in acceleration was associated with hamstring activation before ground contact and eccentric hamstring strength, n = 14 (Morin 2015)

research: Nordic hamstring exercise in injury-prevention programmes: injury risk ratio 0.49 (0.32-0.74) across 15 studies (van Dyk 2019); lower NHE volumes gave similar strength and fascicle adaptations (Cuthbert 2020 meta-analysis)

research: plyometric programmes: sprint gains were most likely with a mix of jump types, horizontal jumps, at least 15 sessions and more than 80 combined jumps per session; added weight gave no extra benefit (Sáez de Villarreal 2012, abstract); resisted sprinting improved linear sprint (SMD 0.65) especially 0-10 m (Li 2025 meta-analysis)

research: strength gains were greater with loads of 80% 1RM or more (up to 8 repetitions maximum) (Lopez 2021); rests of at least 2 min were advised for resistance-trained people for strength (Grgic 2018, abstract)
practice: pattern priorities, 4 x 3-6 heavy sets, 20-30 jump contacts to start and building up, the order of sessions; no paper gives a safe jump progression for a beginner

plyo.reps: 5 jumps (start with 20-30 contacts in total, add about 10 a week toward 80 or more)

speed.tempo: full recovery, stop when speed drops

sessions.name: lower-body strength
sessions.why: Lower-body strength is the base of sprint power: in the research, bigger gains in squat strength went with bigger sprint gains. Heavy sets with long rests build the force part; hinge and hip-extension work targets the muscles that drive acceleration.
sessions.check: Bar speed or rep speed should stay fast; stop a set when the last rep slows a lot. Note the weight and reps.

sessions.name: power and hamstrings
sessions.why: Jumps train the stiff, springy contacts of sprinting, and strong hamstrings that can absorb force are linked to horizontal force and fewer hamstring injuries. Keep the jumps fresh: stop when landings get noisy.
sessions.check: Landings quiet, jumps as high or far at the end as at the start. No sharp hamstring or Achilles pain.

sessions.name: upper body and trunk
sessions.why: Upper-body and trunk strength supports arm drive and keeps the trunk stiff while the legs produce force.
sessions.check: Controlled reps, no shoulder pain.

general.label: General strength and muscle (health, shape, all-round fitness)
basis: research: more weekly sets gave more muscle growth (graded dose-response, Schoenfeld 2017) and more strength (Ralston 2017); at least 4 weekly sets per muscle group in a 6-15 RM range is a minimum for time-efficient training (Iversen 2021)

research: hypertrophy was similar with light and heavy loads when sets are taken close to failure, strength gains were larger with loads of 80% 1RM or more (Lopez 2021); training to failure was not shown to be better than stopping short for hypertrophy (Refalo 2023)
research: when weekly volume is equal, frequency made no clear difference to strength (Grgic 2018; Cuthbert 2021 in well-trained people)
practice: pattern split and the weekly set targets

sessions.name: lower body
sessions.why: Large muscle groups of the legs respond well to weekly sets across squat, hinge and single-leg patterns.
sessions.check: Last 1-3 reps hard. Note the weight and reps.

sessions.name: push and trunk
sessions.why: Pressing patterns and the shoulders get their own weekly sets.
sessions.check: Controlled reps, no shoulder pain.

sessions.name: pull and posterior chain
sessions.why: Rowing and pulling patterns balance the pressing work and protect the shoulders.
sessions.check: Controlled reps, shoulder blades moving.

runner_distance.label: Runner, 5 km to half marathon: better running economy and race pace
basis: research: strength training with resistance and plyometric exercises, 2-3 times a week for 8-12 weeks, improved running economy in highly trained middle- and long-distance runners (SMD -1.42, 5 controlled trials, 93 runners); the programmes used 2-4 lower-body exercises, up to 200 jumps and 5-10 short sprints (Balsalobre-Fernandez 2016)

research: heavy resistance training with near-maximal loads (>= 90% 1RM) improved running economy and time-trial performance more than plyometrics or lower loads (22 studies, g -0.32 vs -0.13); longer programmes (10-14 weeks) worked better (Eihara 2022 meta-analysis)

research: high-load (>= 80% 1RM) and combined methods improved running performance (ES -0.469 and -1.035); none improved VO2max, vVO2max, maximal steady state or sprint capacity (Llanos-Lagos 2024 systematic review; certainty very low to moderate)
practice: which patterns, the 5-8 rep range for athletes who cannot load heavy, and the jump contacts per session

sessions.name: lower-body strength
sessions.why: Heavy lower-body strength is the best-supported way to lower the energy cost of running in trained runners. Few exercises, hard sets, long rests.
sessions.check: Last reps slow but clean, 1-3 in reserve. Note the weight and reps.

sessions.name: power and trunk
sessions.why: Short, springy jumps and calf work train the stiffness and power of the push-off; trunk work keeps form late in a run. Keep contacts low and landings quiet.
sessions.check: Landings quiet, calves not sore the next day. Stop jumps when form gets sloppy.

runner_marathon.label: Runner, first marathon or high weekly mileage: finish healthy, with limited extra training time
basis: research (small RCT): 8 weeks of 2 strength sessions a week in marathon preparation raised knee-extension strength, with no clear difference in running economy or VO2 against endurance alone (22 recreational runners, Ferrauti 2010)

research (RCT, 720 first-time marathoners): a 10-minute quadriceps, hip-abductor and core programme 3 times a week did NOT reduce overuse injuries that stopped the marathon (7.1% vs 7.3%, risk ratio 0.97) (Toresdahl 2020); so no injury-prevention promise is made
research: hip-abductor weakness was linked to iliotibial band syndrome in distance runners, with no clear link for other injuries (Mucha 2017, systematic review)
research: strength training helped running economy in trained runners (Balsalobre-Fernandez 2016) but those runners had more training experience than most first-timers
practice: short sessions placed away from long runs; hip, calf and trunk selection

sessions.name: legs and hips
sessions.why: Strong legs and hips are linked to a stable running stride. Keep it short: the evidence for injury prevention is mixed, so the goal is steady strength without adding fatigue to long runs.
sessions.check: Fresh the next morning; if long-run legs feel heavy, drop to 2 sets or skip a session.

sessions.name: trunk and upper body
sessions.why: Posture and arm swing hold up late in a long run when the trunk and upper back are strong.
sessions.check: Controlled reps, no shoulder pain.

runner_trail_ultra.label: Trail and ultra running: economy, durability on climbs and descents
basis: research (RCT, 25 ultra-marathoners): 12 weeks of home-based strength, explosive and plyometric training lowered the cost of running by 3-6% at submaximal speeds; the authors advise at least three such sessions a week (Giovanelli 2017)
research: strength training improved running economy in trained runners (Balsalobre-Fernandez 2016; Eihara 2022; Llanos-Lagos 2024)
gap: no trial read on eccentric or downhill-specific strength training for trail runners; the step-down and single-leg selection is practice, based on the load that descents put on the quadriceps
practice: three short sessions rather than two long ones; slow eccentric work and calf stiffness before races with big descents

sessions.name: strength
sessions.why: Heavy-ish single-leg and hinge work is the strength part of the programme that lowered running cost in ultra-marathoners.
sessions.check: Last reps slow, 2-3 in reserve. Note the weights.

sessions.name: explosive and plyometric
sessions.why: Short, quiet jumps and hill sprints train the spring of the stride, the explosive and plyometric parts of the programme that lowered running cost.
sessions.check: Quiet landings, calves recover within a day.

sessions.name: descent control and trunk
sessions.why: Long descents load the quadriceps eccentrically; slow step-downs and hip work prepare the legs. (Practice: no trial read on this.)
sessions.check: Knees tracking straight, no pain on the stairs the next day.

runner_middle_distance.label: Runner, 800 m to 5 km racing: economy plus the power for kicks and surges
basis: research: high-load (>= 80% 1RM) and combined strength methods improved running performance in middle- and long-distance runners; none improved sprint capacity, vVO2max or maximal steady state (Llanos-Lagos 2024 systematic review)

research: resistance plus plyometric training improved running economy in highly trained middle-distance runners (Balsalobre-Fernandez 2016); heavy near-maximal loads beat plyometrics for economy and time trial (2022 meta-analysis)
research: elite sprinters do strength and power work 2-3 times a week; resisted and unresisted sprint training both improved linear sprint (Haugen 2019; Li 2025) - used here for the speed slot only
practice: one speed or power day on top of two strength days; loads and jumps as in the runner profile

speed.tempo: full recovery, stop when speed drops

sessions.name: heavy lower body
sessions.why: Heavy loading was the strength method with a clear running-performance effect in middle- and long-distance runners.
sessions.check: Rep speed stays fast; stop a set when it slows a lot.

sessions.name: power and speed
sessions.why: Jumps and short sprints keep the fast-twitch side of middle-distance running trained, because strength training alone did not raise sprint capacity in the review.
sessions.check: Fresh and fast; quality over quantity.

sessions.name: upper body and trunk
sessions.why: Trunk and arm strength supports form at pace.
sessions.check: Controlled reps.

cyclist_road.label: Cyclist, road endurance (sportive, gran fondo, time trial): more power at the same effort
basis: research (RCT, 20 well-trained cyclists): 12 weeks of 4 lower-body exercises, 3 x 4-10 RM, twice a week raised thigh muscle size, maximal force, Wingate peak power, power at 2 mmol/l lactate and mean power in a 40-minute all-out trial (Ronnestad 2010)
research (RCT, 20 elite cyclists): 10 weeks of heavy strength training raised half-squat force and 30-s Wingate power; the 40-minute trial change was not significantly different (Ronnestad 2017)

research (systematic review, 5 RCTs, highly trained cyclists): the 3 studies that improved time-trial performance replaced part of the endurance training with strength work, and 2 of them used explosive exercises; the 2 studies that simply added strength on top did not improve (Yamamoto 2010)
research (review): heavy strength training is recommended for cycling economy; effects on lactate-threshold power are mixed (Ronnestad & Mujika 2014)
practice: fit the sessions in by trimming easy riding (the planner keeps the weekly ride minutes; shorten an easy ride on strength days if you feel flat)

sessions.name: lower body, heavy
sessions.why: Heavy lower-body work raised cycling power measures in the trials: four exercises, 3 sets of 4-10 repetitions, twice a week.
sessions.check: Last reps hard but clean; legs fresh for the next ride within 24 h.

sessions.name: lower body, explosive and trunk
sessions.why: Explosive exercises were part of the strength programmes that improved time-trial performance; the trunk holds the position on the bike.
sessions.check: Explosive reps stay fast.

cyclist_sprint.label: Cyclist, sprint and punch (criterium, track sprint, finishing sprint): peak power and force
basis: research (cross-sectional, 20-30 sprint cyclists): maximum isometric strength was strongly correlated with jump and Wingate power, coach's rank and standing-start sprint times; larger, stronger riders had an advantage (Stone 2004) - a correlation, not a training trial
research (RCTs in well-trained and elite cyclists): 10-12 weeks of heavy lower-body strength training raised 30-s Wingate power more than endurance training alone (Ronnestad 2010, 2017)

research: sprint-power training in running athletes uses heavy sets with long rests, jumps and short sprints (Haugen 2019; Seitz 2014; Saez de Villarreal 2012) - borrowed here as practice, because no cycling-specific jump trial was read
practice: 3 sessions with the sprint work itself done on the bike (the planner does not write bike sprints in this profile)

plyo.reps: 5 jumps (start at 20-30 jumps, add about 10 a week)

sessions.name: maximal strength
sessions.why: Maximal strength correlated with sprint-cycling speed and heavy training raised Wingate power in trained cyclists.
sessions.check: Rep speed stays high; note the weights.

sessions.name: explosive power
sessions.why: Fast, springy work keeps the force quick; quiet landings and full recovery between sets.
sessions.check: Jumps as high at the end as at the start.

sessions.name: upper body and trunk
sessions.why: A stiff trunk and strong arms let the legs push harder against the bars in a sprint.
sessions.check: Controlled reps.

cyclist_bone_health.label: Cyclist (especially masters or high-hour riders): protect bone and keep muscle, a low-impact sport
basis: research (cross-sectional, 40 competitive male cyclists): weight training hours were the only predictor of higher spine and hip bone density; cycling hours and years were not (Mathis & Caputo 2018) - an association, not a trial
gap: no trial read on jumping or heavy lifting to raise bone density in cyclists; the combination of heavy loading and small jumps is practice, with jumps added slowly
research: strength training improved cycling power measures (Ronnestad 2010, 2017); it does not conflict with the goal

plyo.reps: 5 jumps (start with 15-20 jumps in total, add slowly)

sessions.name: weight-bearing lower body
sessions.why: Cycling puts little load through the spine and hips; heavy-ish weight-bearing exercises add the missing load.
sessions.check: Controlled reps; note the weights.

sessions.name: impact, upper back and trunk
sessions.why: Small jumps add impact, and upper-back work balances the bent riding position.
sessions.check: Landings soft; no joint pain.

triathlon.label: Triathlon (long distance): better cycling and running economy across a 26-week block
basis: research (RCT, 25 long-distance triathletes): 26 weeks of strength training, first moderate (8-12 reps, up to 75% 1RM, weeks 0-12) then heavy (1-6 reps, 85% 1RM or more, weeks 14-26), improved maximal strength, cycling economy and running economy with no body-mass change; endurance-only did not improve economy (Luckin-Baldwin 2021)
research: cyclists and runners both gained from heavy strength work (see the runner and cyclist profiles)
practice: the planner switches the heavy prescription at program week 13; set preferences.strength.program_start to the first week of the block

sessions.name: lower body
sessions.why: The triathlete trial improved both cycling and running economy with lower-body strength that moved from moderate to heavy loads.
sessions.check: Note the weights; legs recover before the next key session.

sessions.name: upper body and trunk
sessions.why: Swimming and posture on the bike and the run need upper-back and trunk strength.
sessions.check: Controlled reps, shoulders happy.
